paras: The attempted lynching of Senobio Martinez took place on the Medina in Bexar County, Texas, in April 1882, when a mob of unknown men took Martinez, a Mexican man, from his house at night and hanged him from a tree. Martinez survived by holding the rope above his head for about six hours until friends cut him down, and the San Antonio Express story of his ordeal was reprinted as far away as Pennsylvania and Tennessee.

According to the San Antonio Express, Martinez lived on the Medina and had long incurred his neighbors' displeasure because he was suspected of taking other people's horses and selling them. The Express set the story against the days of the county's vigilance committee, "when Mexican horse thieves might be seen hanging from the limbs of adjacent trees on almost any day in the week."

On a Tuesday night the mob went to his house, took him away, hung him to a tree and left him for dead. Because the men had not tied his hands, he held the rope around his neck with both hands for six hours and was cut down the next day by friends. He could not say who the men were or how many there had been.

Martinez then came to San Antonio, badly bruised about the neck and face, where he told his story. A Dallas Herald special printed on April 21 said he had been hung "yesterday", which together with the Express's "Tuesday night" places the hanging around April 18, though no report gives a calendar date.

After he was brought to the city he stayed with friends on the Alazan creek near town. Judge Felix G. Smith granted an application to send him to the poorhouse for care, but Martinez refused to go, "fearing that the mob would hunt him there and accomplish their foul purpose." No report of arrests, an investigation or a trial appears in the coverage.

The Dallas Herald ran the news as a two-sentence item in a column of San Antonio specials, between a reported earthquake near Fredericksburg and a farmer bitten by a mad mule, first in its daily and then in its weekly edition. The longer San Antonio Express account called the hanging an "outrage" and Martinez "the poor fellow", while repeating the neighbors' horse-theft suspicion and recalling vigilance-era hangings of Mexicans.

Under headlines such as "Hanged for Six Hours" and "Hanging for Six Hours", the Express story was reprinted in the Cambria Freeman of Ebensburg, Pennsylvania, on May 5, the Juniata Sentinel and Republican on May 24, the Bolivar Bulletin on June 1 and the Milan Exchange on June 3. The Cambria Freeman's text placed the Medina in "Baxter county", while the Tennessee and Juniata versions named Bexar County.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Senobio Martinez
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A mob of unknown men took Martinez from his house and hanged him from a tree as a suspected horse thief; he survived (A4, A6, A2).

Martinez survived the hanging, so no one was killed; the attack by 'a mob of unknown men' on a man suspected of horse theft was an attempted lynching (A4, A6, A2). The victim was described as Mexican, not Black (A4, A2).

A Dallas Herald San Antonio special and the San Antonio Express story, separately written, agree that a mob hung Martinez and he survived about six hours, though both rest on his own statement (A2, A4, A6).

accounts.label: San Antonio Express (victim's story)
accounts.gist: Neighbors suspected him of stealing horses; on Tuesday night a mob of unknown men took him from his house and hung him to a tree; friends cut him down the next day; he refused the poorhouse for fear of the mob.

framing.detail: The Express called the hanging an 'outrage' and 'foul purpose' and Martinez 'the poor fellow', while repeating the horse-theft suspicion and recalling vigilance-committee hangings with some relish.
The Dallas Herald special was a two-sentence news item between an earthquake report and a mad-mule bite.
Pennsylvania and Tennessee weeklies reprinted the Express story as 'Hanged for Six Hours' or 'Hanging for Six Hours' from May into June.

versions.value: 'yesterday' relative to a San Antonio special printed April 21 (daily), whose weekly text carries a dateline read as 'April 29'

conflicts.note: The 'April 29' dateline is later than both Dallas issue dates and is likely misprinted or misread; the April 21 printing and 'Tuesday night' fit Tuesday, April 18, 1882, but no text gives a calendar date.
'Baxter' is very likely a printer's or OCR variant of Bexar; the Medina and San Antonio are named in all versions.
